newsitem.title: USA: Costa Rica, El Salvador take varied reform paths.
newsitem.headline: Costa Rica, El Salvador take varied reform paths.

text.p: Officials from Costa Rica and El Salvador on Thursday pledged to liberalise their Central American countries' economies, but offered different perspectives on the prospects for privatisation.

Addressing U.S. investors at the Americas Society in New York, Costa Rican Planning Minister Leonardo Garnier said he saw more compelling investment opportunities in tourism and technology than in privatisation of government firms.
Garnier said that while he saw economic benefits to privatisation, 80 percent to 90 percent of Costa Ricans oppose selling off the state electric and phone companies.
"Privatization is a word Costa Ricans don't like very much, and there are good reasons for that," he said.
He said most Costa Ricans, when asked about the national health care system, would favour improving the system rather than putting it in private hands.
"What you have to be very careful when you talk about concessions and public policy is to do it right, because there have been successful examples and tragic examples," he said.
El Salvador's commissioner for public-sector modernisation, Alfredo Mena Lagos, said his country's government was committed to further deregulatation and privatisation.
He said that despite recent electoral losses by the ruling ARENA party, the opposition did not have enough votes to override a presidential veto.
In March, the leftist FMLN party, made up of former guerrillas, posted significant gains in the 84-member National Assembly, capturing 27 seats, compared with 28 seats for ARENA.

"Reforms that are in place are safe," Mena Lagos said, adding that the sale of the electrical sector would proceed. Privatisation plans for ports, airports and roads will require further discussion, he said.

Mena Lagos asserted that El Salvador would respect its financial commitments, particularly in terms of repaying its foreign debt. He urged investors to ignore talk in the legislature of rolling back the reform process.

"The noise coming out of the assembly is just that: political noise," Mena Lagos said. "You cannot expect anything better from a person who has been in the mountains holding a rifle and shooting, and that does not have the faintest idea that you have to pay your debts."
